thread.title: San Antonio companies are disclosing loads of new details about worker pay. Too bad critics say it's mostly pointless.

author: Jeff Jeffrey
title: San Antonio companies are disclosing loads of new details about worker pay. Too bad critics say it's mostly pointless.
text: Aug 3, 2018, 2:14pm CDT Updated Aug 3, 2018, 2:30pm CDT The U.S. government aimed to expose companies paying big money to CEOs while doling out peanuts to typical employees. What it got was a garbled mix of data and disclaimers with little clarity around the supposed pay disparities plaguing American workers. This year marks the first time the nation's largest publicly traded companies are required to disclose CEO-to-median worker compensation ratios in compliance with the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010. Yet little outrage — or action — has ensued since the numbers began rolling in, largely because companies have done their darndest to take advantage of the mandate’s loose reporting requirements. For the 10 largest CEO-to-median employee compensation ratios among public companies nationwide, click on the slideshow above. To see the same ratios for San Antonio-based public companies, read further for a slideshow below. Analysts and compensation experts say the vague disclosures that have followed make it pointless to compare company ratios or median pay figures, even when looking at major employers in the same industry. “Without context, the ratio is fairly useless,” said Ethan Rouen , assistant professor of business administration at Harvard University whose dissertation focused on pay disparities. “Simply looking at what the CEO makes and what some random employee makes doesn’t provide a clear picture. It’s really a missed opportunity to address the very real issue of income inequality.” Disclosures among major retailers have been particularly uneven. For example, Target Corp. (NYSE: TGT) included thousands of non-U.S. employees to determine its CEO-to-median worker pay ratio, while Home Depot Inc. (NYSE: HD) excluded more than 15,000 foreign workers while still including thousands of Canadian employees. McDonald’s (NYSE: MCD) determined its median employee was a worker in Poland earning $7,017 per year, whereas Yum! Brands Inc. (NYSE: YUM), which owns KFC, Pizza Hut and Taco Bell , excluded more than 2,000 employees, or about 4 percent of its workforce, in Brazil, Canada and France. Jessica Schieder , an analyst at the Economic Policy Institute , said the exclusion of international employees can significantly sway a pay ratio, especially for companies in developing nations. She said ratios for U.S. and international employees should be broken out separately. Many San Antonio-based public companies calculated their median compensated employees based on the compensation of all employees, foreign and domestic. Biglari Holdings Inc. (NYSE: BH, BH.A) had the highest CEO-to-employee pay ratio at 828-to-1 in San Antonio, based on its median employee being a part-time worker. At the same time, Biglari excluded its international workforce because it accounted for less than 5 percent of the total. “Another important factor is that companies are not required to annualize their data. You also don’t know whether a company is going to use the same calculation method next year,” Schieder said. The challenges extend beyond geography and timing. At pharmacy giant CVS Health Corp. (NYSE: CVS), median employee pay included the company's share of health and retirement benefits. Dozens of other companies, including clothing and home goods retailer The TJX Cos. Inc. (NYSE: TJX), were more circumspect and did not disclose the factors that go into a typical worker's pay. In San Antonio, many public companies calculated median employee compensation with benefits, although how the compensation was presented differed. Companies like Valero Energy Corp. (NYSE: VLO) displayed the median employees compensation similarly to the CEO, with salary, nonequity incentive plans, changes in pension and all other compensation itemized, while companies like Cullen/Frost Bankers Inc. (NYSE: CFR) and Rush Enterprises Inc. (NASDAQ: RUSHA, RUSHB) showed only the median employee's total compensation. Still, other companies went to lengths in explaining why their operations and methods in calculating pay ratios differ from the competition. In a recent filing, Walmart Inc. (NYSE: WMT) noted its “unique” position as the world’s largest retailer, with roughly 2.3 million workers. “Therefore, our reported pay ratio may not be comparable to that reported by other companies … in calculating their respective pay ratios,” the company said. In calculating its CEO-to-median pay ratio of 1,188-to-1, Walmart excluded nearly 90,000 workers outside the U.S. Walmart's median worker earned $19,177 per year as of 2017, versus the $22.8 million compensation package awarded to CEO Doug McMillon last year. Context required A key loophole in Dodd-Frank allows companies to exclude up to 5 percent of international employees from their ratio calculations. That, among the law's other nuances, has prompted many companies to warn that “the ratio reported by other companies may not be comparable," as was the case in Yum! Brands' recent filings with federal regulators. Many San Antonio-based public companies made similar statements regarding the variance in how the median employee was calculated. Harvard's Rouen said the disclosures also fail to account for the varied ways companies do business and compensate top executives. He pointed to Google's parent company, Alphabet Inc. (Nasdaq: GOOGL), which pays CEO Larry Page a $1 salary, and Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL), which differs from other device and phone makers in that it operates its own portfolio of retail locations, as difficult companies to draw comparisons to. Also, Rouen said companies have to balance paying CEOs enough to keep them from leaving with keeping investors happy. TJX Cos. has a 1,500-to-1 pay ratio, "which can appear pretty startling,” Rouen said. “But it depends on who’s interpreting it. [CEO Ernie Herrman] has performed brilliantly there. The stock price has increased 50 percent under his leadership.” Similarly, many San Antonio CEOs received sizable boosts in compensation in the form of stock awards, including Joseph Gorder at Valero; Gregory Goff at Andeavor (NYSE: ANDV), which is being acquired by Marathon Petroleum Corp. (NYSE: MPC); and William Stacy Locke at Pioneer Energy Services Corp. (NYSE: PES), all of whom had stock awards as their highest area of compensation. Rob Du Boff, the director of corporate research at JUST Capital, said that while companies differ in their calculations, the disclosures are better than nothing. He said more information will ultimately inform workers and help companies establish more competitive workplace practices. “A little more context would be beneficial,” he said. “But in addition to salary, many workers are increasingly concerned about things like work-life balance. People want to know how companies treat their employees beyond what they pay them.”
